slides.title: From chromatin footprints to gene regulatory networksReproducible methods for integrative regulatory genomics
slides.notes_text:
Good morning, and thank you for being here.
Today I’ll present my dissertation, “From chromatin footprints to gene regulatory networks.”
The central goal of this work is to develop reproducible methods that move from open chromatin, to TF-binding prediction, and finally to link target genes.

slides.title: A simple view of transcriptional regulation
slides.notes_text: I’ll start with a simple view of transcriptional regulation. When chromatin is open, transcription factors can bind DNA and help recruit RNA polymerase II, which initiates transcription. This brings us to two main questions: where do transcription factors bind, and which genes do they regulate?

slides.title: Transcription factors recognize specific DNA sequence motifs
slides.notes_text:
Let’s start with the first question: where do TFs bind?
First, the DNA needs to be accessible. Then a transcription factor can bind.
But TFs do not bind DNA randomly. They recognize short DNA sequence patterns called motifs, like the sequence logo shown here.
Different TFs prefer different motifs. For example, HNF4A, GATA, SOX, and AP-1 each have their own sequence preference.
These known motifs are collected in databases such as JASPAR and HOCOMOCO.
So motifs tell us where a TF could bind, but not whether it is actually bound.
But there is another problem: different TFs can recognize very similar motifs.

slides.title: TF motifs cluster into related families
slides.notes_text:
Here, I took the JASPAR motifs and grouped them by sequence similarity.
In the center is the full motif collection, and around the outside you can see that similar motifs naturally form families, such as Forkhead, Homeobox, and bHLH, and other TF families
The important point is that TFs within the same family can recognize very similar DNA sequences.
So a motif may tell us the TF family, but not necessarily the exact TF that is bound.
To identify the specific TF, we need TF-specific experimental measurements

slides.title: Protein-specific assays provide direct evidence of TF binding
slides.notes_text:
Here are three common TF-specific assays.
On the left, ChIP-seq uses an antibody to pull down DNA associated with the TF.
In the middle, CUT&RUN uses the antibody to recruit a nuclease and cut nearby DNA.
On the right, CUT&Tag uses the antibody to recruit Tn5 and cut and tag nearby DNA.
Different mechanisms, but the same goal: after sequencing, we identify where that TF is bound.
These assays give us much stronger TF-binding evidence than motif matching alone

slides.title: Experimental challenges in measuring TF binding
slides.notes_text:
The problem is scale.
We have many TFs, but these are targeted assays, so each TF usually needs its own experiment. 
That quickly becomes many experiments, and it also depends on having a good TF-specific antibody. 
More experiments means more time and cost. 
So we need a more scalable way to study TF binding. 
That brings us to ATAC-seq.

slides.title: ATAC-seq maps open chromatin
slides.notes_text:
ATAC-seq tells us where the chromatin is open.
First, we have closed and open chromatin.
Second, Tn5 inserts into the accessible DNA.
After sequencing, those insertions build up into ATAC-seq peaks.
So a high ATAC-seq signal means the chromatin is more accessible.
But if we look inside that peak more closely, the local Tn5 pattern can tell us more about TF binding.
ATAC-seq (Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin using sequencing)

slides.title: ATAC-seq footprinting reveals protected TF-binding sites
slides.notes_text:
Here is the basic idea of ATAC-seq footprinting.
Tn5 can cut the accessible DNA on both sides of the site.
But when a TF is bound in the middle, it protects that DNA, so we see fewer cuts in the center.
That dip in the middle is the footprint.
And on the right, the AP-1 example shows the same pattern in real data — high signal on the sides, and a dip at the motif center.
So footprinting gives us more localized evidence of TF binding than the broad ATAC-seq peak alone.
Then the next question is how to detect&analyze footprints?

slides.title: Gaps in existing ATAC-seq footprinting tools
slides.notes_text:
ATAC-seq footprinting is not new. All of these tools can do the basic bulk footprinting analysis.
Some newer tools also support single-cell analysis and de novo motif discovery.
Our goal with fp-tools was not to replace these methods. 
What fp-tools adds is a footprinting framework that extends TOBIAS with de novo motif discovery, biological-replicate analysis, single-cell workflows, and improved computational efficiency.

slides.title: fp-toolsReproducible ATAC-seq footprinting for bulk and single-cell dataCraftGRN Module 1Predicting condition-specific TF-binding sitesCraftGRN Module 2Predicting TF regulated target genes
slides.notes_text:
The first part of my dissertation is fp-tools, a reproducible ATAC-seq footprinting framework for bulk and single-cell data.
I’ll begin with the overall workflow.

slides.title: fp-tools provides an end-to-end bulk and pseudobulk workflow
slides.notes_text:
Here is the overall fp-tools workflow.
We can start from either bulk ATAC-seq or single-cell ATAC-seq, which we convert into pseudobulk groups.
Both then go through the same core steps: bias correction, footprint calling, and motif matching.
From there, fp-tools can do differential footprinting, de novo motif discovery, and single-cell footprint analysis.
One feature I’ll show next is de novo motif discovery.

slides.title: De novo motif discovery finds patterns missing from reference databases
slides.notes_text:
Here, we start from the footprint regions.
We extract the surrounding DNA sequence, then run de novo motif discovery to find recurring sequence patterns.
After that, we compare those motifs with the reference database.
In the bar plot below, most sites are associated with known motifs, shown in green, but a smaller fraction are de novo-only, shown in orange.
So the reference database captures most of the signal, but not all of it
The next question is whether these de novo motifs also show a real footprint pattern

slides.title: De novo motifs show clear footprint signatures in K562 and HepG2
slides.notes_text:
Here are representative de novo motifs from K562 on the left and HepG2 on the right.
In each example, the motif is centered at zero, and the Tn5 signal shows a clear dip at the motif center, with higher signal on the sides.
That is the footprint pattern we expect.
So these de novo motifs are not just recurring sequence patterns, they are also supported by local footprint signals.
Next, we asked whether footprint activity changes between biological conditions.

slides.title: Differential footprinting highlights TF activity changes between conditions
slides.notes_text:
Here, fp-tools compares footprint activity between two conditions with biological replicates.
Before comparison, we can scale the signals across samples; here I used q95 scaling.
On the left, we see the top differential motifs. In the center, the volcano plot shows the overall comparison. And on the right, we can directly inspect the footprint profiles behind those statistics.
In this example, HNF4A and ONECUT2 are stronger in HepG2, while GATA-family footprints are stronger in K562.
So the report connects the statistics directly to the actual footprint patterns
We then applied the same idea to single-cell ATAC-seq.

slides.title: Single-cell footprints recover cell-type-specific TF programs
slides.notes_text:
Here, the cells separate into three broad groups: B cells, monocytes, and T/NK cells.
On the left, B cells show stronger STAT6 and FOSB footprint signatures.
In the middle, monocytes show stronger CEBPA, IRF8, and RELA.
And on the right, T/NK cells show stronger ZNF683, NR4A1, and SMAD3.
So the footprint profiles recover distinct TF programs for different cell types.
Let me show a few of these examples more clearly on the UMAP

slides.title: B-cell footprint signatures highlight STAT6 and FOSB
slides.notes_text:
First, the B-cell population.
Here, STAT6 and FOSB show stronger footprint signals in the B-cell cluster.
You can see the red signal concentrated on the B cells on the left.
So these footprints recover a clear B-cell-associated TF pattern
We see a different pattern in monocytes

slides.title: Monocyte footprint signatures highlight CEBPA, IRF8, and RELA
slides.notes_text:
In monocytes, CEBPA, IRF8, and RELA are much stronger.
The red signal is concentrated in the monocyte cluster on the right.
These TFs are consistent with myeloid and inflammatory regulation.
So the footprint signals again match the expected cell identity.
And the T/NK population shows another distinct pattern

slides.title: T/NK-cell footprints highlight ZNF683, NR4A1, and SMAD3
slides.notes_text:
In T/NK cells, ZNF683, NR4A1, and SMAD3 show stronger footprint signals.
Here, the red signal is concentrated mainly in the central T/NK population.
So across these three cell types, fp-tools recovers distinct TF programs from the same single-cell ATAC-seq dataset.
So fp-tools works in both bulk and single-cell settings. Next, I’ll show the computational performance.

slides.title: fp-tools runs faster and uses less memory
slides.notes_text:
We also improved the computational efficiency of the workflow.
On the left, fp-tools runs faster than TOBIAS.
On the right, it also uses less memory.
So fp-tools is not only more complete, but also lighter and faster to run.
And we also wanted to make it easier to use, not just faster.

slides.title: The fp-tools browser interface makes reproducible workflows easier to use
slides.notes_text:
The browser interface exposes the same fp-tools commands through a webpage.
Users can select an analysis, load an example or enter their own paths, review the YAML configuration, start the run, and inspect the outputs.
Importantly, the GUI does not create a separate analysis path. It launches the same reproducible workflow used by the command line.
So fp-tools makes footprinting more complete, efficient, reproducible, and accessible.
With those footprint measurements in place, I’ll now move to CraftGRN Module 1.

slides.title: fp-toolsReproducible ATAC-seq footprinting for bulk and single-cell dataCraftGRN Module 1Predicting condition-specific TF-binding sitesCraftGRN Module 2Predicting TF regulated target genes
slides.notes_text:
fp-tools tells us where footprint-like signals occur.
CraftGRN Module 1 asks the next question: which TF is most likely responsible for each footprint?

slides.title: TF binding is dynamic and cell-type specific
slides.notes_text:
But assigning a TF to a footprint is not straightforward, because TF binding is highly dependent on biological context.
The same genomic site can be occupied in one cell type but not another. And even within the same cell type, binding can change between biological conditions. So TF binding is dynamic and cell-type specific. 
A static sequence motif alone cannot capture that context.
And context is only one part of the problem. The DNA sequences recognized by TFs are also more flexible than a single canonical motif.

slides.title: TF binding extends beyond canonical motifs
slides.notes_text:
A TF may have a preferred canonical motif, but real binding is more complicated.
TFs can recognize motif variants, bind cooperatively with another TF at composite sites, or be recruited indirectly through tethering without contacting their own motif.
So canonical motif matching alone cannot explain every TF-binding event.
We can see that limitation directly in our HNF4A data.

slides.title: HNF4A binding extends beyond canonical motif matches
slides.notes_text:
Here I’m using HNF4A in HPAF-II pancreatic cancer cells as a representative example.
The purple signal is the independent HNF4A CUT&Tag measurement, the purple bars mark called peaks, and the orange bars mark canonical HNF4A motif matches.
Several strong HNF4A peaks do not contain a canonical motif match.
This shows that motif information explains only part of the observed HNF4A binding landscape.

slides.title: Computational approaches for TF-binding prediction
slides.notes_text:
There are three main computational approaches to TF-binding prediction.
First, motif-based methods like FIMO or HOMER search for known TF sequence motifs and then treat motif matching as TF binding.
Second, footprinting methods like TOBIAS and HINT-ATAC treat footprint + motif matching as TF binding. 
Third, supervised models such as EPCOT learn from existing TF-binding data. EPCOT uses DNA sequence and cell-type-specific ATAC to predict TF binding. It can generalize to new cell types, but only for the TFs learned by the pretrained model, and its predictions are at one-kilobase resolution, rather than individual footprints. And limited to generalize to new cell types.
So what we still need is a way to assign candidate TFs directly at footprint resolution, using the biological context of our own samples.
That is the problem addressed by CraftGRN Module 1.

slides.title: CraftGRN Module 1 assigns candidate TFs to footprinted sites
slides.notes_text:
Module 1 uses matched ATAC-seq and RNA-seq across the same biological conditions.
We begin with a footprint and use motif information to define plausible TF candidates. We then compare the footprint activity with each candidate TF’s expression across conditions.
When TF expression and footprint activity vary together, that relationship provides condition-specific support for the TF–footprint pair. When they do not vary together, the pair is not retained.
For supported footprints, we can then expand the search to the broader set of expressed TFs.

slides.title: Redundant footprint calls are merged before TF-binding prediction
slides.notes_text:
Before predicting TF binding, we first remove redundancy.
Different motif annotations can produce several overlapping calls over the same underlying footprint. Treating all of those calls as independent would overcount the region.
CraftGRN therefore merges overlapping calls into a single nonredundant footprint, while retaining the original motif-family information for downstream analysis.

slides.title: Consolidation reduces redundancy and reveals more diverse TF families
slides.notes_text:
Here I compare the same number of top-ranked footprints before and after consolidation.
Before consolidation, many top calls are repeated observations from the same motif or TF families. After consolidation, those repeated calls are reduced.
As a result, the top footprint set represents a broader and less redundant collection of TF families.
This gives us a cleaner starting point for TF-binding prediction.

slides.title: Footprint signal improves TF-binding prediction
slides.notes_text:
Before showing the comparison, I’ll briefly define the main metrics.
Recall, or true-positive rate, is the fraction of experimentally detected binding sites that we recover. Precision is the fraction of our predictions that are experimentally supported. The false-positive rate measures how often we incorrectly predict binding at negative sites.
In the curves below, blue uses the correlation between TF expression and the broad ATAC-seq signal. Orange uses the correlation with the localized footprint signal.
In both the MAFF and HNF4G benchmarks, the footprint-based approach gives higher true-positive rates and higher precision.
So the localized footprint signal is more informative for TF-binding prediction than accessibility alone.

slides.title: Top footprint-ranked sites contain more true TF-binding predictions
slides.notes_text:
Here I focus only on the top-ranked predictions.
Green represents true positives, and orange represents false positives. As we move from the top 30,000 predictions toward the top 5,000, the footprint-based ranking contains a progressively higher proportion of true positives.
Compared with the ATAC-based ranking, the footprint ranking contains fewer false positives, especially among the highest-ranked sites.
Based on this result, we use footprint activity as the main regulatory signal in the downstream CraftGRN predictions.

slides.title: CraftGRN performs consistently across pancreatic TF-binding datasets
slides.notes_text:
We then compared the complete CraftGRN method with EPCOT. Orange is CraftGRN, and gray is EPCOT.
Here are two representative benchmarks: MAFF in HPAF-II and HNF4G in AsPC1.
CraftGRN is comparable to or better than EPCOT in the ROC curves, but the clearest gain is in the precision–recall curves.

slides.title: CraftGRN maintains higher precision across additional pancreatic TFs
slides.notes_text:
The same pattern appears for HNF4A and KLF5.
CraftGRN again gives similar or better ROC performance, while maintaining higher precision across a broad range of recall.
Taken together, these benchmarks show a consistent precision advantage across multiple pancreatic TF-binding datasets.
We next asked whether CraftGRN was also recovering the stronger experimental binding events.

slides.title: CraftGRN preferentially recovers stronger TF-binding events
slides.notes_text:
Here, the solid lines represent true positives and the dashed lines represent false negatives. Orange is CraftGRN, and gray is EPCOT.
Across most benchmarks, the true-positive sites recovered by CraftGRN have stronger experimental TF-binding signal than the true positives recovered by EPCOT.
At the same time, the sites missed by CraftGRN generally have weaker signals.
So CraftGRN is not only recovering more supported sites—it is preferentially recovering the stronger binding events, while many of the remaining false negatives are weaker.

slides.title: CraftGRN recovers experimentally supported TF-binding sites across TFs and cell lines
slides.notes_text:
Here I show a set of representative loci: two each for HNF4A in AsPC1, KLF5 in HPAF-II, and FOSL2 in HPAC.
In each panel, we compare the ATAC signal, the experimental binding assay, the detected sites, and predictions from CraftGRN and EPCOT.
Across these loci, CraftGRN predictions track the experimentally detected binding sites more closely, while EPCOT tends to produce more dispersed predictions.
So at the genomic-region level, we again see that CraftGRN gives more precise TF-binding predictions across different pancreatic TFs and cell lines.

slides.title: CraftGRN performs well in an independent T-cell dataset
slides.notes_text:
So far, the main benchmarks have come from pancreatic cancer systems. We next tested whether the same framework performs well in an independent biological context.
Here we use T-cell ChIP-seq for ETS1, IRF4, and JUND as the experimental reference. Orange is CraftGRN, and gray is EPCOT.
Across the three TFs, CraftGRN is comparable to or better than EPCOT in ROC performance, with the clearest precision gains for ETS1 and IRF4.
These results indicate that Module 1 is not limited to the pancreatic cancer datasets.

slides.title: CraftGRN covers more TFs with lower computational cost
slides.notes_text:
Beyond prediction accuracy, we also compared computational practicality.
CraftGRN runs faster on CPU, uses less memory, and can evaluate a substantially broader set of expressed TFs. EPCOT can benefit from GPU acceleration, but its outputs remain limited to the TFs supported by the pretrained model.
So Module 1 combines broader TF coverage, lower computational cost, and competitive or improved prediction performance.
That completes the first prediction task: identifying likely TF-binding sites. The next question is which genes those sites regulate.

slides.title: fp-toolsReproducible ATAC-seq footprinting for bulk and single-cell dataCraftGRN Module 1Predicting condition-specific TF-binding sitesCraftGRN Module 2Predicting TF regulated target genes
slides.notes_text:
Module 1 tells us where a TF is likely to bind.
CraftGRN Module 2 asks the next question: which gene is that TF likely to regulate?

slides.title: Experimental methods for linking TF-binding sites to target genes
slides.notes_text:
A predicted TF-binding site does not automatically identify its target gene.
Experimentally, there are two major types of evidence we can use.
One is TF perturbation followed by RNA-seq. We knock down, knock out, or overexpress a TF and look for genes that change. But these experiments are time-consuming and costly, and the expression changes can include both direct and indirect effects. A real target can also be missed if regulation depends on multiple TFs, if another TF compensates, or if we measure at the wrong time point.
The other is 3D chromatin interaction data, such as Hi-C or HiChIP. These assays can provide evidence of physical contact, but they are also resource-intensive, their resolution can be broad, and physical contact does not necessarily imply functional regulation.
That is why computational methods combine different types of evidence to predict target genes are needed.

slides.title: Computational methods for linking TF to target genes
slides.notes_text:
Computationally, there are several common strategies.
The simplest is proximity—for example, linking a binding site to the nearest gene or to genes within a TSS window. This is easy to apply, but it can miss distal regulation.
A second approach uses 3D contact information or regulatory priors. Hi-C and HiChIP provide physical-contact information, while models such as ABC and ENCODE-rE2G combine multiple features to predict enhancer–gene relationships. 
Co-accessibility approaches ask whether regulatory regions and promoters show coordinated chromatin changes across cells or samples.
Finally, Integrated models such as Taiji, GRaNIE, and SCENIC+ combine accessibility, expression, motif, and other regulatory evidence.
The important point is that these approaches use different types of evidence, and no single strategy is ideal for every dataset.
CraftGRN Module 2 follows the same idea: use the predicted TF-binding sites from Module 1, then combine genomic distance with matched multi-omic evidence and optional regulatory priors to identify likely target genes
Back up: integrated models combine multiple data types. For example, Taiji uses chromatin accessibility, motif and gene expression to build regulatory networks; GRaNIE integrates open chromatin with RNA-seq; and SCENIC+ combines single-cell chromatin accessibility, gene expression, and motif-based regulatory information.

slides.title: CraftGRN Module 2 uses proximity and correlation to predict target genes
slides.notes_text:
So rather than relying on only one type of evidence, CraftGRN combines the information available in our matched datasets
Module 2 begins with the TF-binding sites predicted by Module 1.
For each site, we identify nearby candidate genes within a genomic window. If three-dimensional interaction information is available, it can be used as an additional prior.
Across matched biological conditions, we then ask two questions: does target-gene expression track with TF expression, and does it also track with footprint activity?
When both relationships provide support, the TF–binding-site–gene relationship is retained as a predicted TF–target gene link.
We then evaluated whether these predicted targets respond in independent TF-perturbation experiments.

slides.title: CraftGRN recovers perturbation-supported SOX9 and KLF5 targets
slides.notes_text:
Panels A and B use independent siRNA RNA-seq experiments for SOX9 and KLF5.
CraftGRN shows substantially higher precision than Taiji and GRaNIE. As we focus on the top-ranked CraftGRN targets, those genes also show stronger downregulation after TF knockdown.
Panels C and D summarize the predicted networks. The central red node is SOX9 or KLF5, the blue boxes are additional TFs, and the gray circles are genes.
The important result is not simply that some TFs appear close together on the plot. The edges show that these TFs connect to overlapping sets of predicted target genes.
This suggests convergence on shared downstream genes, which is consistent with combinatorial regulation, rather than each TF acting independently.
We next tested Module 2 outside the pancreatic cancer system.

slides.title: CraftGRN recovers IRF4-responsive targets in an independent T-cell dataset
slides.notes_text:
Here we tested Module 2 in an independent T-cell dataset with IRF4 overexpression.
In the ROC and precision–recall curves, CraftGRN clearly outperforms Taiji and GRaNIE.
And on the right, the top CraftGRN predictions are increasingly enriched for genes that are strongly upregulated after IRF4 overexpression. So the ranking is putting the most IRF4-responsive genes near the top.
We then looked at how these predicted IRF4 targets fit into the broader T-cell regulatory network.

slides.title: IRF4, BATF, RUNX3, and T-bet converge on shared T-cell target genes
slides.notes_text:
In this network, IRF4 is connected with BATF, RUNX3, and T-bet, or TBX21, through overlapping sets of predicted target genes.
These TFs connect to overlapping predicted target genes.
That interpretation is biologically plausible because T-cell regulation is highly combinatorial. IRF4 and BATF cooperate in T-cell regulatory programs, while RUNX3 and T-bet are major regulators of T-cell differentiation and effector function.
So CraftGRN recovers a coordinated multi-TF regulatory program, rather than treating each TF as an isolated regulator.
I’ll now summarize the main contributions of the dissertation.

slides.title: Conclusion
slides.notes_text:
To summarize, this work makes three connected contributions.
First, fp-tools provides reproducible and efficient ATAC-seq footprinting for bulk and single-cell data.
Second, CraftGRN Module 1 combines footprints, motifs, and TF expression to predict condition-specific TF-binding sites.
Third, CraftGRN Module 2 combines genomic proximity with matched regulatory evidence to predict likely target genes.
Independent TF-binding and perturbation datasets support these predictions across pancreatic cancer and T-cell systems.
Overall, fp-tools and CraftGRN provide an integrated path from chromatin accessibility, to TF binding, and finally to predicted gene regulation.
These results also point to several future directions.

slides.title: Future Directions
slides.notes_text:
There are three main directions for extending this work.
First, because footprint performance depends on the TF, future versions could select or combine footprint callers based on TF-specific performance.
Second, CraftGRN can be extended from condition-level analysis to cell-state-resolved networks using single-cell multiome data.
Third, Module 3 will focus on differential regulatory programs—identifying coordinated TF–gene programs that change across biological conditions.
Finally, I’d like to acknowledge the people who made this work possible.

slides.title: Backup slides
Gaps in existing ATAC-seq footprinting tools
slides.notes_text:
novelty:
fp-tools extends interpretable TOBIAS-style footprinting into a faster, replicate-aware, single-cell-capable, de novo-motif-aware, and fully reproducible analysis platform.
Compared with the TOBIAS-style baseline, fp-tools adds or extends:
Improved computational efficiency
Faster execution and lower peak memory in the matched benchmark. 
De novo motif discovery integrated with footprint analysis
Candidate footprints can be exported, analyzed with MEME/DREME/STREME, compared with known motifs using Tomtom, and carried back into downstream analysis. 
Biological-replicate differential footprinting
Per-replicate motif scores, replicate summaries, empirical-Bayes moderated testing, and multiple-testing correction rather than treating conditions as single profiles. 
Cross-sample footprint normalization and scaled aggregation
Including shared-background q95 scaling for multi-sample comparisons. 
Integrated pseudobulk single-cell workflow
Grouped scATAC fragments can enter the same core footprint pipeline, with cell-level KNN-smoothed footprint signatures for visualization. 
Interactive and publication-oriented reporting
Interactive HTML reports, linked motif/footprint views, and editable SVG export. 
Reproducible execution surfaces
Command line, saved YAML configurations, browser GUI, run history, and auditable analysis settings. 
Orthogonal validation framework
The full workflow was benchmarked against matched TF ChIP-seq across 12 TF–cell-line comparisons in five cancer cell lines; footprint-score AUROC exceeded PWM AUROC in 10 of 12 comparisons.

slides.title: CraftGRN recovers HNF4A binding beyond canonical motif matches
slides.notes_text:
Here I’m showing representative HNF4A loci. The purple track is the independent CUT&Tag signal, the orange marks are canonical motif-supported sites, and the blue marks are CraftGRN predictions.
You can see that CraftGRN recovers many binding sites that are not captured by canonical motif matching alone. This is exactly the advantage we were aiming for: extending TF assignment beyond canonical motif matches while still keeping the predictions anchored to footprint activity and matched TF expression.

slides.title: CraftGRN recovers TF-binding sites near epithelial and adaptive-response genes
slides.notes_text:
These tracks show what the predictions look like at individual genomic regions in HPAF-II cells.
Blue is the ATAC-seq signal, purple is the independent TF-specific signal and detected peak calls, orange is CraftGRN, and gray is EPCOT. The gene models below provide the local genomic context.
Across regions near EPCAM, JUP, VIL1, ELF3, EGR1, PCK2, and JAG1, CraftGRN predictions align closely with experimentally detected TF-binding sites.
These genes are associated with epithelial identity, junction organization, stress response, metabolism, and Notch-related signaling.
At this stage, the gene names provide genomic context; the actual target-gene assignment comes later in Module 2.

slides.title: CraftGRN recovers multi-TF binding near epithelial and survival genes
slides.notes_text:
We see similar locus-level agreement in AsPC1 across several TF families, including HNF4A, FOSL1, FOSL2, HNF4G, and KLF5.
CraftGRN recovers experimentally supported binding sites near genes associated with epithelial identity and polarity, such as EPCAM, LGALS4, ELF3, PARD6B, and MUC17, as well as adaptive-response genes such as BNIP3L and EGR1.
The key result is agreement at individual binding sites across multiple TFs, rather than only an improvement in aggregate performance.

slides.title: CraftGRN recovers FOSL2 binding near invasion and epithelial genes
slides.notes_text:
This slide focuses on FOSL2 binding in HPAC cells.
CraftGRN recovers experimentally supported sites near genes involved in invasion and remodeling, such as MMP7; metabolic adaptation, such as PCK2; AP-1 feedback, including FOS and JUND; and epithelial adhesion and polarity, including CDH1, CLDN3, CLDN7, and PARD6B.
Again, these are binding-site predictions near biologically relevant genes. They do not yet establish that every nearby gene is directly regulated by FOSL2.
